full_judgment:
21. As to proceedings under section 145 CrPC it is erroneous to designate the complainant as an informant, having regard to the provisions of that section. Once an information is brought to the notice of the Magistrate he has to be satisfied that a dispute as to immovable property is likely to cause a breach of the peace. Further proceedings which he starts are not proceedings in the interest of any private party but in the interest of public peace. (See Babu Vs. Shyam, ILR 1950 All 543). It is, therefore, highly doubtful if a proceeding under section 145 CrPC can properly be termed as a "criminal matter" within the meaning of section 56 (e) of the Specific Relief Act. 

 31. In a decision of the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Sajjan Singh, son of Jahan Nath Singh Vs. Sajjan Singh, son of Bharu Singh and another, 1970 UJ (SC) 75 (the Law Report being not available, the gist of the decision has been taken from the "Twenty-one years' Supreme Court Digest 1950-70" by SK Agarwal Volume 2 (1972) at page 662), the facts were that in a proceeding under section 145 CrPC the Sub-Divisional Magistrate ordered the attachment of the house in question. While the appellant's application to the Sub-Divisional Magistrate to drop the proceeding was pending, he filed a civil suit for permanent injunction so that his own possession might not be disturbed. A temporary injunction was granted on the following day. He produced the order of temporary injunction and asked for stay of the proceeding under section 145 CrPC. The Sub-Divisional Magistrate dismissed the application and ordered the Tashildar to take over the house as a receiver. Against the order of the Sub-Divisional Magistrate a revision was filed in the Court of Sessions. The Sessions Judge made a Reference to the High Court recommending that the appointment of the receiver be set aside. The High Court came to the conclusion that both the order of attachment of the house and the appointment of the receiver were valid and that the civil Court's order of temporary injunction had no effect upon the proceeding before the Sub-Divisional Magistrate.
